notes: Ceiling effect: the no-skill baseline scored 20/21 (95%). Sonnet 5 already handles these rail / modal-trap / Back-stack tasks well from base knowledge, so the measurable lift from the skill is a single assertion (eval 2: stating the dialog should take initial focus on open and the background should stop showing a highlight). This suite does not isolate where the skill adds value.
Non-discriminating assertion: eval 1 #8 ("no DOM focus model introduced") cannot realistically fail on a bespoke DOM-less fixture — both runs pass it trivially.
Ambiguous assertion: eval 1 #5 ("...and ideally bubble at the edge") — the baseline kept return true at the horizontal edges and still passed; the "ideally" clause makes it unenforceable.
Cost of loading the skill: with_skill runs averaged ~+22s wall time and ~+13k tokens (reading SKILL.md + 4 reference files). Single-run sample, large time stddev — treat as rough.

Grader provenance error: the eval-3 grader claimed the skill "is an unpopulated placeholder." It is populated; the with_skill executor read and cited the reference files. Pass/fail counts are unaffected.

Qualitative signal (not captured by pass rate): where counts tie, the with_skill answers consistently pull in specific skill framing — the 5-level Back priority table, "the exit hint must stay out of the focus tree," "reset a rail index to 0 when its data is swapped," defaulting a destructive confirm to Cancel, and treating focus restore as a generic focus-path walk rather than a hardcoded target.

For a next iteration that actually measures the skill: target cases a strong baseline gets wrong — focus memory after a data refresh, ragged last-row clamping in a grid, stacked-modal restore order, geometric-vs-index strategy choice, focus guides for layout gaps — or accept this as a guidance-quality skill better judged qualitatively than by pass rate.
